shipped_rows.title_o: Do female and ethnically diverse executives endure inequity in the CEO position or do they benefit from their minority status? An empirical examination

blind_target.evidence_quote: With the goal of contributing to cumulative knowledge development in this area, we seek to reexamine Hill et al.'s finding about gender differences in CEO compensation by extending the analyses further in time, using a larger sample of firms and more rigorous empirical analyses.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Recently, Hill, Upadhyay and Beekun reported that female CEOs receive greater compensation than male CEOs, which runs counter to common wisdom that the gender pay gap in the labor market favors men over women. With the goal of contributing to cumulative knowledge development in this area, we seek to reexamine Hill et al.'s finding about gender differences in CEO compensation by extending the analyses further in time, using a larger sample of firms and more rigorous empirical analyses. Our findings, which are robust to different statistical procedures and econometric specifications, do not reveal reliable evidence for differences in compensation paid to male and female CEOs.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The abstract explicitly identifies the earlier female pay advantage and finds no reliable difference. Expanded firms and years support replication rather than exclusively reanalysis of original data. No reference list accessible, so full citation title and initials are unavailable.

luna_triage.reason: The abstract identifies the target as Hill, Upadhyay and Beekun's finding that female CEOs received greater compensation than male CEOs, and says it reexamines that finding using later years and a larger sample. The supplied row 1151 has the same three authors and describes the CEO minority-status/inequity examination that reported this finding. The source title dates Hill et al.'s work to 2015, while the shipped row gives 2014, consistent with online-first versus issue-year dating of the same article; it is not a distinct target.
